1.6.idea: A decision between "lesion" and "background" is a decision between two noisy populations. Their separation, measured in units of the noise, is the only thing that matters when the noise is roughly Gaussian and the same in both: the overlap of two bell curves $\mu$ and $\mu+\Delta$ with common $\sigma$ depends on $\Delta/\sigma$ alone. Contrast alone (the numerator) ignores how large the fluctuations are; SNR alone ignores how different the object is from its surroundings. Averaging $n$ independent pixels, or frames, divides $\sigma$ by $\sqrt n$, which is how a large lesion becomes visible at the same CNR per pixel.

2.9.idea: Each pixel's Beer–Lambert exponent (imaging-2.3) is a sum over the materials crossed; at two energies the bone/tissue ratio differs because bone's photoelectric absorption falls faster with energy than tissue's (imaging-2.4), so the two equations are independent and the $2\times2$ system is invertible. Noise from counting statistics (Poisson, imaging-1.7) in $A_1$ and $A_2$ is propagated through the matrix inverse, and a nearly singular matrix magnifies it, producing a noisier subtraction than either original image.
vizLabelReplacements: (condition number $${fx(st.cond, 1)}$): the further apart $E_1,E_2$, the better conditioned the inversion.
(row-angle proxy $${fx(st.cond, 1)}$): this proxy measures near-parallel rows, not the relative condition number.

3.7.idea: Polar coordinates in the inverse 2-D Fourier transform supply the Jacobian |ω|. The slice theorem replaces each radial Fourier restriction by the corresponding projection transform; its inverse transform is qθ, and the remaining angle integral is back-projection. In the continuous full-band model this inverts the 1/r blur. A finite Nyquist cutoff limits resolution, and sampled edges introduce aliasing. Kak & Slaney §3.3.3 explicitly distinguish the finite kernel's nonzero DFT value at DC from simply sampling |ω| and forcing its DC bin to zero; zero-padding permits the desired aperiodic convolution over the retained detector samples.

3.8.idea: Reconstruction is linear, so noise in the sinogram passes through the same filter-and-back-project operation as the signal. White noise in the projections has a flat spectrum; after the ramp its spectrum grows as $\omega^2$, so variance comes mostly from the highest frequencies. A window removes those frequencies — less variance, and a lower modulation transfer (imaging-1.4) at fine scale. The reconstruction's point spread function is the Fourier transform of the windowed filter, so the window also fixes the edge sharpness measured here.

3.11.idea:
For any solution $z$ of a consistent system, one update gives
$$\|x^+-z\|^2=\|x-z\|^2-\lambda(2-\lambda)\frac{(b_i-\mathbf a_i\cdot x)^2}{\|\mathbf a_i\|^2}.$$
Thus distances to every solution decrease or stay fixed. Summing this identity makes successive corrections tend to zero; cyclic visitation then makes every row residual tend to zero. Boundedness gives a solution cluster point, and the same distance identity forces convergence to it. Every correction lies in the row space, so the null-space component of the start is preserved: the limit is its closest solution. For mutually orthogonal independent rows, $\lambda=1$ reaches that solution in one complete pass, not one row step. Row order and angles affect speed; no filter or positivity projection is used here.
3.11.ideaPrefix:
For any solution $z$ of a consistent system, put $r_i=b_i-\mathbf a_i\cdot x$. One update gives
$$\begin{aligned}\|x^+-z\|^2&=\|x-z\|^2\\&\quad-\lambda(2-\lambda)\frac{r_i^2}{\|\mathbf a_i\|^2}.\end{aligned}$$
Thus distances to every solution decrease or stay fixed. Summing this identity makes successive corrections tend to zero; cyclic visitation then makes every row residual tend to zero. For mutually orthogonal independent rows, $\lambda=1$ reaches that solution in one complete pass, not one row step. Row order and angles affect speed; no filter or positivity projection is used here.

3.12.idea:
The normalization gives a direct convergence proof for the stated SIRT variant. Set $B=R^{1/2}AC^{1/2}$ and $y=C^{-1/2}\mu$. Weighted Cauchy–Schwarz yields
$$\|Bz\|^2\le\sum_i\sum_j a_{ij}z_j^2/c_j=\|z\|^2.$$
The update becomes $y^+=y+\lambda B^T(R^{1/2}b-By)$. Each positive singular mode contracts by $1-\lambda\sigma^2\in(-1,1)$, while null components remain fixed, proving the weighted least-squares claim. Small singular values make some modes slow and can amplify noise in the limit. SART's view blocks use updated images between views; this SIRT proof does not assert that an inconsistent cyclic SART run has the same limit. Kak–Slaney Eq.32 supplies the view-wise normalization, but the illustration deliberately omits their bilinear basis and longitudinal Hamming weighting.

4.7.idea: The survival probabilities of the two photons are exponentials of path integrals over complementary pieces of the line, and the exponent of a product is the sum of exponents, $\int_0^t+\int_t^\ell=\int_0^\ell$. The depth variable cancels. This is the Beer–Lambert law (imaging-2.2) applied twice, and it is the reason PET is quantitative: one measured number per LOR, a ray sum of $\mu$ as in imaging-3.1, corrects the emission data exactly (for narrow-beam, scatter-free photons), whereas SPECT (4.5) needs the whole $\mu$ map and gets only an approximate correction.
